title: BlueNebula x Redwood - Partner Intro & Discovery
summary: Introductory partner discovery call between Redwood (AE+SE) and BlueNebula. Discussed BlueNebula's edge GPU footprint, interest in marketplace listings and a private deployment option for enterprise customers, potential joint benchmarks, and commercial/ops model. Security and data residency are key for BlueNebula customers. Agreed next steps: share security docs, draft integration scoping, schedule pilot benchmarks, and pricing outline.
action_items: Alex Kim - send partner intro deck + Redwood partner one-pager - due 2026-06-15
Priya Patel - share benchmark template and sample KV cache config notes - due 2026-06-16
Miguel Santos (BlueNebula) - share infra spec (GPU types, network topology) and example tenant reqs - due 2026-06-18
Samir Rao - confirm initial pilot customer and timeline (Q3) - due 2026-06-19
next_steps: Redwood to upload SOC2 + security FAQ link to shared folder
Schedule technical deep-dive (SE-led) next week to go over VPC/private control plane options
Align on pilot scope and pick 1 joint customer for benchmarks
Exchange pricing models and marketplace listing requirements
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. This is Alex from Redwood, AE on the partnership side. We have Priya, our solutions engineer, with us. How's it going at BlueNebula?
[00:20] Samir Rao: Hey Alex, good thanks. This is Samir, head of partnerships. We also have Lena and Miguel on the line. Appreciate you making time.
[00:25] Alex Kim: Awesome. Quick round robin, then we'll dive into what each org is looking to get out of a collab. Priya, do you want to say hi?
[00:30] Priya Patel: Hi all, Priya here — I work on integrations and performance at Redwood. We'll be the technical lead if we move forward.
[00:35] Lena Ortiz: Hey, Lena. I'm product at BlueNebula. We're focused on edge GPU infra for media and LLM workloads.
[00:40] Miguel Santos: Miguel here, infra. I run the clusters and network.
[00:45] Alex Kim: Great. High level — Redwood provides a unified inference platform that customers can use hosted, on dedicated reserved capacity, or as a private deployment behind a VPC. We care about predictable latency and cost controls. For partners, we do marketplace listings and joint go-to-market plus technical integrations.
[01:05] Samir Rao: Good, that's exactly what we wanted to hear. We have customers asking for a turnkey model hosting or a managed private control plane that sits in their VPC. We're exploring two paths: list BlueNebula in Redwood's marketplace as a compute option, and also evaluate a private deploy for a couple enterprise customers.
[01:25] Alex Kim: Makes sense. Can you say more about the BlueNebula infra — GPU types, regions, and how you expose capacity — and any constraints?
[01:35] Miguel Santos: Sure. We run A100 and H100 variants, mixed nodes — some 80GB and some 40GB. Our footprint's in US-East, US-West, and EMEA. We offer tenancy models: shared multi-tenant pools and dedicated racks for enterprise. Network is 100GbE in the fabric, with overlay for customer isolation.
[01:55] Priya Patel: Do you offer an API for scheduling or is it more of a managed toggle?
[02:00] Miguel Santos: We have an API, but it's relatively new. For some enterprise deals we do a managed pipeline where we provision dedicated racks and a private control plane.
[02:10] Alex Kim: Good; that aligns well. For marketplace use-case, customers commonly want to spin up Redwood-hosted endpoints that run on partner infra under the hood. For private deploys we can run Redwood Private — control plane still in customer or partner VPC and compute in BlueNebula.
[02:30] Lena Ortiz: One concern — data residency and keys. Many of our customers need KMS and customer-managed keys; they also want audit logs.
[02:40] Priya Patel: We support KMS integrations and audit logs, yes. Our Private option supports HSM/KMS integrations and the console surfaces per-route tracing and token-level cost breakdowns.
[02:55] Miguel Santos: When you say private, do you mean the control plane is customer-managed or Redwood still manages control plane but in their VPC?
[03:05] Priya Patel: We have both options. There's a fully customer-managed on-prem package and a private control plane pattern where we run the control plane in the customer's VPC but Redwood still does management under contractual terms. We can clarify which model fits your customers.
[03:20] Alex Kim: On the performance side, Priya, can you walk through typical benchmarks and what we measure?
[03:25] Priya Patel: Sure, we typically measure p95 latency for generation at common sequence lengths, throughput for batch workloads, and token cost per 1k tokens with different batching and KV cache strategies. We also look at cold vs warm KV cache hit rates and memory footprints when using quantized models.
[03:45] Samir Rao: Would be good to see a sample benchmark doc — some partners send spreadsheets for side-by-side.
[03:50] Priya Patel: We'll share our benchmark template. It includes model configs, sequence lengths, hardware used, and a standard prompt set. Also, we can run a joint benchmark on your H100 80GB nodes.
[04:05] Lena Ortiz: What about fallback and routing? If a customer uses Redwood and you hit capacity on our side, can Redwood route to alternative regions or model variants?
[04:15] Alex Kim: Yes, smart routing is a core feature. Policy can be by latency, cost, or region. We also have automatic fallback to compatible model variants when capacity is constrained. In partner setups we can route to either partner pools or Redwood Dedicated pools.
[04:30] Miguel Santos: Okay. Another angle is billing and commercial model. Does Redwood do pass-through billing or do you want partners to invoice?
[04:40] Alex Kim: We support multiple models. For marketplace flows we can handle billing through Redwood and pay partners a take for compute, or partners can invoice customers directly for dedicated/private deals. We typically negotiate for pilot/commercial terms during the partner onboarding.
[04:55] Samir Rao: Sounds flexible. Security checklist — our enterprise customers frequently ask for SOC2, SAML SSO, RBAC, and encryption at rest with customer KMS. Do you have docs for those?
[05:10] Priya Patel: Yes, we have a security FAQ and SOC2 reports. We'll drop the links. A caveat: sometimes automated transcription makes 'SAML' show up as 'samal' — but yes, SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning are supported.
[05:25] Lena Ortiz: Great. Network topology question: for private control plane, does Redwood require a VPN or can you do VPC peering?
[05:35] Priya Patel: We support multiple networking patterns: private endpoints through VPC peering, AWS Transit, or site-to-site VPN. For stricter customers we can recommend VPC peering plus private subnets for control plane components.
[05:50] Miguel Santos: Latency targets — what SLOs can you commit for typical LLM inference?
[05:55] Alex Kim: We publish performance profiles for our verified models; SLOs vary by deployment. For hosted public endpoints p95 might be 200-400ms for short generations but with heavy batching it can increase. For dedicated/reserved setups with optimized kernels we can aim for sub-200ms p95 for many models. We'll share our model catalog performance sheet.
[06:20] Samir Rao: That would help when we position to customers. Another integration route: managed marketplace listing where BlueNebula shows as compute option in Redwood's provisioning flow. What's required on your side?
[06:35] Priya Patel: We ask partners for an image or AMI/container spec, API endpoints for provisioning, credentials or a mechanism for transient credentials, and a small integration shim that handles autoscaling hooks and health checks. We have a partner integration guide.
[06:55] Lena Ortiz: On autoscaling, we usually expose an API for autoscaler decisions; does Redwood expect push or pull?
[07:05] Priya Patel: We can support either. Many partners implement a metrics pull where Redwood's runtime queries capacity; others have a webhook push for scale events.
[07:15] Miguel Santos: For capacity planning, our rack provisioning lead time is around two weeks for dedicated racks if we need to reconfigure, but for pre-warmed nodes we can be faster.
[07:25] Alex Kim: Helpful. On the go-to-market side, Samir, what are you thinking — co-sells, marketplace discoverability, joint webinars?
[07:35] Samir Rao: All of the above. We want to show customers a clear path: they can pick BlueNebula compute in Redwood console or opt for a BlueNebula-managed private deployment with Redwood powering inference. Initial focus would be media customers and enterprise LLM hosts.
[07:50] Alex Kim: Good. We'll propose a joint webinar and a case study once the pilot customer's results are in.
[07:58] Lena Ortiz: Quick question on observability — does Redwood provide per-request traces and token-level cost breakdowns? Customers ask for that for billing reconciliation.
[08:08] Priya Patel: Yes. Redwood Console shows per-route/model dashboards, tracing hooks, token-level cost/latency breakdowns and error analysis. We also have export options to Datadog or S3 for raw traces.
[08:25] Miguel Santos: Any concerns about KV cache and stateful sessions? Some of our customers run long chat sessions and want cache locality.
[08:35] Priya Patel: We handle KV cache management and can colocate caches to improve locality. It's a common topic — caching helps token cost and latency. For cross-region cases we might keep KV caches warm in the region to avoid cross-region pulls.
[08:50] Samir Rao: On compliance, our enterprise customers sometimes require customer-managed HSMs. Is that supported?
[08:58] Priya Patel: We integrate with KMS and HSMs depending on the deployment pattern. For full on-prem or private deployments we can support customer-managed HSM. We'll note that in the security doc.
[09:10] Alex Kim: Ok, let's surface some risks/tradeoffs: 1) latency vs cost — partnering means some customers will accept slightly higher latency for lower cost or better data residency; 2) operational corollaries — who owns the runbooks and on-call for incidents; 3) billing reconciliation.
[09:30] Lena Ortiz: For runbooks, BlueNebula handles hardware incidents, Redwood handles runtime incidents; we should document the handoff.
[09:38] Miguel Santos: Agreed. We also need to define escalation paths.
[09:43] Alex Kim: We'll draft an ops SLA and on-call matrix as part of partner onboarding.
[09:48] Samir Rao: Great. Any technical red flags from Priya?
[09:52] Priya Patel: Nothing critical — we'd like to see an API sample for provisioning, your AMI/container spec, and a short runbook for node health checks. Also we'd prefer to run an initial set of benchmarks on representative workloads.
[10:10] Lena Ortiz: We can share that. We'll also share a whitepaper we've used for customers about GPU zoning and noisy neighbor mitigation.
[10:18] Alex Kim: Perfect. We'll kick off a small pilot: Redwood will spin up a single model endpoint on BlueNebula H100-80GB, run a 1k-prompt benchmark suite, and document p95/p99 latencies, throughput, and token cost.
[10:35] Miguel Santos: Timeline-wise we can provision nodes in 3-5 business days for a pilot.
[10:40] Alex Kim: Good. Back to commercial: do you have a target rev share or margin expectation for marketplace listings?
[10:48] Samir Rao: We typically look at 60/40 gross margin thresholds and want to ensure partner economics aren't squeezed. But flexible depending on volume.
[10:55] Alex Kim: We'll prepare a pricing outline — marketplace take rates vs dedicated contract models and present both options.
[11:05] Priya Patel: I also want to call out edge cases: if a customer needs air-gapped on-prem, Redwood can support an on-prem package, but there is more setup and a different licensing model.
[11:20] Lena Ortiz: Understood. We'll flag which customers might need that.
[11:25] Alex Kim: Ok let's recap actions and next steps.
[11:28] Alex Kim: Redwood: send partner deck, SOC2 and security FAQ, benchmark template. Priya will send sample KV cache config and API integration guide.
[11:38] Samir Rao: BlueNebula: share infra spec, AMI/container artifacts, and identify pilot customer.
[11:45] Lena Ortiz: We'll also prepare a short runbook and the whitepaper Miguel mentioned.
[11:50] Miguel Santos: I'll send an infra spreadsheet with GPU types, network topology, and provisioning lead times.
[11:58] Alex Kim: Let's schedule a technical deep dive next week — SE-led. How's Wednesday 10am PT?
12:03 Samir Rao: That works for us.
[12:05] Alex Kim: Great, we'll send an invite and include a draft agenda (integration hooks, network patterns, benchmark plan). Any final questions?
[12:15] Jia Chen: One minor thing — support for custom model images. Can Redwood host partner-provided model images?
[12:22] Priya Patel: Yes, we support partner or customer-provided model artifacts; we can host images or point to partner registries. We'll need to vet the images for compatibility and security.
[12:35] Alex Kim: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the items discussed.
[12:40] Samir Rao: Thanks all, excited to move forward.
[12:44] Lena Ortiz: Thanks.
[12:46] Miguel Santos: Bye.
